coherence.reasons: X answers first and groups its case under three pillars (economics fail, cannot afford to find out, software is the better route). Its slide 3 maps five 'would have to be true' conditions to those sections, and each slide title states a quantified claim that its evidence supports. Y is also logically ordered (five sub-questions to five sections to a recommendation), but with small mismatches. Its section finding 'loses money even before the dark store is paid for' is evidenced with the after-site-cost figure. Its basket-by-rider grid is shown before site costs under a title saying orders 'pay their own way', which sits awkwardly with the governing thought that no observed case makes money. X's equivalent grid is at site level and at best density, so it directly supports its claim.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion: do not launch, scale the software, sell a store-based fast-delivery module, and set gates for reopening. X weighs more alternatives: launch, single-store pilot, software plus module, status quo, a second pop-up and a hybrid, scored on path to profit, runway, exposure, downside and reversibility. It also stress-tests its own recommendation at 45% and 30% growth and with opex up 10% a year, names the assumption that matters most, and flags founder focus and channel conflict. Y weighs three options and rejects the one-store test with a runway calculation, but it does not stress the software path beyond stating the 60% assumption. Y's gates are sensible, and its 'capex funded outside the $12.0M' gate is a good one. X's 'no extra fee' trigger is somewhat arbitrary given the Zipcart evidence. Overall X's trade-off treatment is more complete.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: median −$6.17, best composite −$1.76, pop-up −$12.57, plan +$2.02, and $2.5M or about 6 months of runway at month 18. Both also apply Zipcart's levers to the median and get −$1.05. Neither computes the best-density-with-fee case (about +$2.25), so both engage only partly with the evidence that favours the founders. X states the 41.5% CAGR explicitly; Y gives only 'about 40%' and the year-on-year rates. X adds a site-level break-even grid at best density, break-even basket sizes of $50 and $63, both readings of the $9.5M budget, and a customer acquisition bill to fill the stores, with assumptions flagged. Y adds a useful one-input-at-median test of the plan and a 20% sensitivity table. Y's grid, however, is before site costs, and it asserts that the best basket and best rider productivity came from different sites, where the pack says this only of basket and density. X has a few stretched inferences: that the median order-level result sitting between the incumbents 'supports the benchmarks', and a $37M first-year need that assumes full volume from day one. These are labelled. X uses the critical evidence slightly more fully and precisely.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis on the right grounds and avoid the traps. They separate growth from profitability, show that even best observed density loses money, treat the pop-up's growth as promotion-led, discount the survey, and contextualise the Zipcart proof point. X handles the hypothesis more explicitly. It states it, breaks it into five testable conditions, grades the market condition 'partly met', tests 'we run them better than anyone' against the pop-up, and gives fair caveats that the pop-up was a six-week early read. Y concedes the growth claim and honestly marks 'nobody owns the Midwest' as untested, but its treatment of the hypothesis is implicit rather than structured. Both leave the door open through reopening gates rather than a flat no.

overall.reasons: Both documents are sound and reach the same defensible recommendation with correct core numbers. X would serve the board better for four reasons. Its argument is more tightly structured around the founders' hypothesis. Its unit-economics break-even analysis is at site level. It tests the runway under both readings of the $9.5M. It stress-tests the software alternative and compares more options. Y is competent and has some good touches: the one-input-at-median test, named owners for next steps, and a gate requiring capex funded outside the $12.0M. But it is less rigorous on the robustness of its own recommendation and has minor inconsistencies between claims and evidence.
